opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I'd say tool use in Llama 3 is a real step, but it's an early step, and I want to be honest about that. What we focused on was making the model genuinely good at calling tools in a zero-shot way: search, code execution with a Python interpreter, Wolfram Alpha for math, and then being able to generalize to tools it has never seen, just from a function definition in the prompt. That last part is the important one, because you can't anticipate every API a developer will plug in.

A lot of the work was on the data side. You can't just scrape tool-use trajectories from the web, they don't really exist at scale. So we had to build them: synthetic data, human annotation on multi-step trajectories, and having annotators judge not just the final answer but the intermediate steps, like was that the right tool to call, was the query to the search engine sensible, did the model correctly read the output and recover when the code threw an error. That error recovery piece is underrated. An agent isn't something that never fails; it's something that notices it failed and adapts.

Now, as a step toward agents: I think of tool use as the foundation. If the model can't reliably call a function, parse the result, and decide what to do next, there's no point talking about long-horizon autonomous agents. With Llama 3 we got to the point where single-step and short multi-step tool use is quite solid. Where it's still weak, and where the whole field is still weak honestly, is long horizon planning, keeping a coherent goal over dozens of steps, and knowing when to stop or ask for help.

So my assessment is: necessary but not sufficient. The next big leaps, I believe, come from training on the agentic loop itself, with more RL-style feedback from the environment rather than only imitation of human trajectories. That's where I'm most excited for the next versions.

r001.rationale: The response describes Llama 3’s tool use as an early foundation for agents and says short multi-step tool use is solid. It does not clearly characterize that behavior as occurring across multiple messages.

fable-5.1.text:
So, I think tool use is one of the things we were really explicit about with Llama 3, and I'd frame it as a necessary step rather than the destination. The way I see it, a language model on its own is a kind of closed system. It has what it learned at training time and nothing else. The moment you give it the ability to call a tool, whether that's a search engine, a code interpreter, Wolfram Alpha, whatever, you break that closed loop. The model can now act on the world and get feedback from it. That's the beginning of agency.

What we did with Llama 3 was train it natively for this. Zero-shot tool use, where the model gets a tool definition it's never seen and can figure out how to call it, and also multi-step tool use where it has to chain calls, look at an output, decide what to do next. We spent a lot of effort on the data side there, because the hard part isn't the format, it's the judgment. When should you call a tool, when should you not, how do you recover when the tool returns garbage. A lot of the post-training work was about that decision-making rather than the syntax.

Now, am I satisfied? No. I'd say we're at the point where tool use works well in the setting of a single conversation, a handful of calls, a human in the loop. What a real agent needs is to operate over long horizons, to plan, to verify its own work, and to fail gracefully without a human watching. Those are still open problems, and honestly I think they're less about tool calling and more about reasoning and self-correction. The tool is the hand, but you still need the brain to know what to do with it.

The other thing I'd say, and this is something I believe pretty strongly, is that open weights matter a lot here. Agents are going to be built by people composing models with their own tools, their own environments, their own data. You can't do that well behind an API. So for me, Llama 3's tool use isn't just a capability, it's an invitation. We gave you the primitive, now go build the agents, and the next version of the model will learn from what you build.

r001.rationale: The response describes multi-step tool use as chaining calls, examining outputs, and deciding what to do next, and calls tool use the beginning of agency. It places this in a single conversation, which still communicates the criterion’s early multi-step agent behavior across interaction turns.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s an important step, but tool use is only one piece of an agent. A model can be very good at answering a question, and still struggle when it has to decide, “Do I need a tool? Which tool should I use? What do I do with the result?” And then it has to repeat that process reliably over several steps.

So I would look at Llama 3’s tool use as a foundation. The interesting question is not just whether it can make a correct tool call, but whether it can use the feedback to make progress toward a goal, recognize when something went wrong, and recover. That’s the transition from generating an answer to actually completing a task. I think that’s a very promising direction, but I wouldn’t equate tool-use capability with having solved agents.

r001.rationale: The response calls Llama 3’s tool use a foundation and describes repeating the tool-use process over several steps, using feedback, and recovering from errors—an early sign of multi-step agent behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
I think tool use is an important step, but it’s not the whole story. A model can produce a function call, and that’s useful. An agent needs to decide when to call a tool, understand the result, and then decide what to do next. If something fails, it needs to recover.

With Llama 3, I would distinguish the capabilities of the model from what you can build around it. You can build tool-use systems on top of it, but that doesn’t mean you have a reliable agent out of the box. The interesting question is how well it works over a sequence of actions. A small error rate on each step becomes a big problem when you have many steps.

So I see it as a foundation. Tool use gives the model a way to act beyond generating text; reliability over longer tasks is what makes that useful as an agent.

r001.rationale: The response describes tool use as a foundation and discusses reliability over sequences of actions, but it does not characterize Llama 3’s tool use across multiple messages.
